question: What are the most common reasons prospects hesitate to buy?

resolution.read_instruction: Extract every objection, concern, reservation, or reason the prospect gives for not buying, delaying, or hesitating on OrbitFlow (including pricing, budget, security, integrations, timing, internal approval, competing tools, and implementation effort), along with any stated context on how the prospect framed it and how OrbitFlow staff responded.
assumptions: 'Prospects' interpreted as Prospect call type (new business) only, excluding Renewal, Churn post-mortem, and Cold call calls.
'Most common' requires aggregating reasons across calls, so each call is read for its underlying stated objections rather than for a frequency count.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: It's more than I expected. And I know why — I'd mentally benchmarked this against Zapier, which is not a fair comparison
findings.context: Pricing was higher than the prospect expected, anchored on Zapier as a benchmark. — Customer framed it as more than expected; acknowledged the Zapier comparison is unfair but still the number in her head. Vendor responded by deferring a number until user model is known.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: But I'd need a clearer ROI story than "it saves time."
findings.context: Prospect could justify the price only with a clearer ROI story than time savings, and may need to offset Gainsight spend. — Customer conditional on replacing enough manual work and possibly retiring Gainsight; vendor deferred pricing discussion.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: The real commercial question is whether we expand the Workato contract we already have instead of adding another vendor.
findings.context: The real blocker is internal: expanding the existing Workato contract instead of adding another vendor. — Customer said the gating issue is not security; the commercial question of Workato expansion is the internal fight she must win. Vendor committed to write it as a pilot exit criterion.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: And the honest comparison is Workato, or just improving what we already have. Not doing nothing.
findings.context: Status quo (Workato or improving existing process) is the honest comparison, and 'do nothing' is not the alternative. — Customer and vendor agreed the pilot should be defined against status quo and alternatives; vendor said 'don't buy OrbitFlow' is a valid outcome.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: I would not sell this internally as headcount reduction. It wouldn't survive contact with my CFO and it's also not true.
findings.context: Prospect will not sell the case internally as headcount reduction; concern about CFO scrutiny. — Customer rejected headcount framing as both unconvincing to CFO and untrue; prefers consistency and speed.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: I do not want to find out in month four that every occasional approver needs a full seat.
findings.context: Concern about per-seat surprises: wants explicit treatment of occasional approvers versus full seats. — Customer worried about month-four surprise; vendor said pricing will be itemised and approval-only users may be structured differently.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: I want to make sure we don't buy a tool that looks great in a demo and then becomes another thing my team has to babysit.
findings.context: Concern that a demo looks great but becomes another thing the team must babysit; wary of hidden scaling and fragility. — Customer's concern about tools that become maintenance burdens and depend on individuals; vendor pointed to run history and ownership features.

findings.speaker: Tom Alvarez
findings.quote: AI's interesting but it's not worth blocking the automation case over.
findings.context: Security review is not a blocker; AI usage and LLM data handling may need separate review and could be scoped out. — Customer said separation would help and AI is not worth blocking automation; vendor offered to disable AI or scope pilot to deterministic steps.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: That last one needs to be in writing. Not in a demo.
findings.context: Prospect requires that no-training on customer workflow content be documented in writing, not just stated in a demo. — Condition for trust; vendor agreed it belongs in the contract.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: And the people who'll operate it have to believe they can own it — that last one is not a small thing.
findings.context: Prospect expects the decision to slip and wants the operating team to believe they can own the workflow. — Timing concern: choose vendor by end of July, first workflows live in September; customer says it will slip. Ownership by operators is a key decision condition.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: I'd want that in the evaluation. A demo with clean data proves nothing to me.
findings.context: Schema change and dirty-data failures are a concern; prospect will only trust a pilot that tests missing data and breakage. — Prior integrations died silently on field renames; vendor recommended explicit validation and error-rate alerts.

findings.speaker: Rachel Morgan
findings.quote: I'm wary of the word agent, mostly because it usually means nobody can explain why something happened.
findings.context: Prospect is wary of AI agents because they can obscure why something happened. — Reservation about agent-style AI; vendor framed AI as optional, inspectable steps.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: The BAA is the gate. If you can't offer one, we cannot use OrbitFlow for any workflow that may involve protected health information.
findings.context: Prospect (security architect) says the BAA is a hard gate; without one, OrbitFlow cannot be used for any workflow that may involve PHI. — Security gate raised first, stated as non-negotiable. Maya declined to give a yes on the call and committed to a written legal/compliance position within a week; Elliot said a verbal 'working on it' is not acceptable.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: The second one. That separation would help a lot, actually. AI is interesting but it's not worth blocking the automation use case over.
findings.context: Prospect's concern about LLM/AI data handling was significant enough to want AI excluded from phase one; they accepted deferring AI review to a separate track. — Elliot called it 'the one I actually care about'. Vendor offered disabling AI or scoping phase one to deterministic steps. Priya noted it was a bigger concession than usual.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: That last sentence. Is it in the contract or is it on a marketing page?
findings.context: Prospect wants a no-training commitment to be contractual, not just marketing-page language. — Vendor said it 'needs to be in the contract for you to rely on it'; Elliot said he will insist on that.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: We're a US operation with a UK subsidiary. What's the default region?
findings.context: Prospect raised US/UK data residency as an open concern, since they are a US company with a UK subsidiary. — Vendor said default region depends on provisioning and would confirm in writing rather than guess.

findings.speaker: Elliot Greene
findings.quote: We will need that conversation. We have workflows where an admin should know a step failed without seeing the record contents.
findings.context: Prospect has concern about vendor staff and workflow run data exposing sensitive patient-adjacent record contents; field-level masking is required. — Vendor said masking is a design conversation, not a checkbox. Priya later said Elliot would have opinions about the run-history screen showing payloads.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: Procurement will not have a serious pricing conversation until security tells us whether the BAA requirement can be met. If the answer's no, the price is irrelevant.
findings.context: Prospect will not engage on pricing until the BAA/security question is resolved; price is irrelevant if the answer is no. — Priya explicitly said this was not a negotiating position. Vendor quoted Growth from $1,800/month and said Enterprise is the relevant tier.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: I don't want to discover in month four that every occasional approver needs a full seat.
findings.context: Prospect is wary of per-seat licensing surprises, especially for occasional approvers and notification-only users. — Vendor declined to quote a figure until a user model is built; said builders and full users are licensed and approvers can be structured differently.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: Power Automate. Or just improving what we already have.
findings.context: Status quo and Microsoft Power Automate are the real competitors; Power Automate is already covered by their Microsoft agreement, which matters to procurement. — Vendor said a 'don't buy' outcome is valid if the existing approach meets criteria more cheaply. Earlier Priya said Power Automate is already covered by the Microsoft agreement.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: A technically correct workflow that everyone routes around is a failed implementation.
findings.context: Prospect worries that adoption will fail, with users routing around a technically correct workflow, as happened with a previous internal tool. — Raised in the pilot-measurement discussion; Priya wants adoption measured alongside technical success.

findings.speaker: Priya Shah
findings.quote: No production launch before Q4. That's firm.
findings.context: Timing constraint: no production launch before Q4; only a non-sensitive proof of concept is possible sooner. A successful pilot would not automatically mean broad deployment. — Priya said pilot and broad deployment are two decisions with different approvers. Vendor said it would rather hear this now.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Eighteen hundred a month is hard for a team our size. I had something closer to eight hundred, maybe a thousand, in my head.
findings.context: Prospect finds Growth price ($1,800/month) hard for a team their size; expected closer to $800-1,000. — Pricing objection raised by Sophie; Leo acknowledged the gap but did not dispute it.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: It's a meaningful discount, not a transformation.
findings.context: Annual prepay discount is meaningful but does not halve the price. — Prospect asked whether annual prepay would materially change the number; vendor said it helps but only partly.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Above that it goes to the COO and the finance director.
findings.context: Budget approval threshold: prospect can only approve tools under $15k/year; the $21.6k annual cost goes to COO and finance director, a slower process. — Internal approval hesitation; the buyer's stated reason for delay.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: budget is the biggest risk here. We could decide we're simply over-buying, and keep Zapier while improving documentation and ownership.
findings.context: Budget is the biggest risk; prospect may conclude they are over-buying and keep Zapier with better documentation and ownership. — Sophie framed a no-buy outcome as legitimate; Leo said he'd rather learn that in July than month five.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: I'm just not yet convinced the value closes the gap between this and the tools we already pay for.
findings.context: Not yet convinced the value closes the gap between OrbitFlow and tools already paid for (Zapier). — Summary of hesitation at end of call; Sophie said she is not saying no.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: If that's a polling hack I'm not interested.
findings.context: Shopify trigger must be native and event-driven; a polling workaround is a dealbreaker. Vendor could not confirm trigger coverage and deferred to a written answer. — Integration concern; vendor did not confirm.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: EU data residency is available on Enterprise. On Growth, I'd need to confirm the default processing region for you in writing rather than guess.
findings.context: EU data residency is only on Enterprise tier; default processing region on Growth is unconfirmed, and Enterprise is the expensive tier. — Security/data-location concern tied to UK/EU customers; vendor deferred on Growth.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Everyone says that and then there's a surprise later.
findings.context: Prospect is wary of hidden usage-based costs for AI features and premium connectors. — Pricing-surprise concern raised about AI digest; vendor offered to model assumptions in writing.

findings.speaker: Marcus Lee
findings.quote: Nobody's ever asked me to count it.
findings.context: Prospect is skeptical of the ROI case; current Zapier spend and maintenance time are not yet quantified, making the business case hard to build. — Internal business case concern; Marcus does not know the cost of current setup; vendor suggested a four-week time log.

findings.speaker: Sophie Reed
findings.quote: Maintenance and visibility. The same two things. Make would give me the branching but I'd still have the ownership problem.
findings.context: Prospect's alternatives are Zapier and Make; the concern is maintenance and visibility, and Make would still leave the ownership problem. — Competitive comparison; vendor framed the bar as beating Zapier plus better documentation.

findings.speaker: Leo Grant
findings.quote: Big-bang migrations of sixty automations is how these projects die.
findings.context: Prospect worries about a big-bang migration of about sixty automations; vendor advised migrating only the three worst first. — Implementation effort concern; reassured by vendor.

findings.speaker: Marcus Lee
findings.quote: Nobody touches anything in November. Company rule.
findings.context: Timing: the team wants automations cleaned up before holiday peak, and a decision is needed by August since nobody changes anything in November. — Timing constraint on buying; implicit deadline.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: Because if the deployment architecture doesn't work, the product is irrelevant. We have bought software before that demonstrated beautifully and then could not reach our systems.
findings.context: Prospect hesitates on deployment architecture: systems that cannot be exposed to the public internet cannot be reached by a platform calling over the internet. — Martin frames this as a gating concern; Jon responds that an agent or controlled gateway pattern may work but must be validated against the actual environment.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: the biggest issue is whether SAP and our on-premise systems make the implementation too heavy for the first use case. Everything else is manageable.
findings.context: Prospect states the biggest issue is whether SAP and on-premise systems make implementation too heavy for the first use case; this is the crux of the decision. — Martin says everything else is manageable; if integration needs nine months of work, he would choose a different first use case or not proceed.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: Six is realistic if the use case is contested.
findings.context: Prospect's works council (Betriebsrat) co-determination could delay the project by about six months if workflows monitor employee activity. — Anika raises it as a non-technology gate; Jon asks a clarifying question and offers designing team-level aggregation to address it.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: It is two hundred and forty questions.
findings.context: Prospect's governance team requires a long list of security and compliance items (SAML, SCIM, audit logs, IP restrictions, private connectivity, DR docs, pen tests, EU data residency) and a 240-question questionnaire before proceeding. — Anika frames it as a normal list, not difficulty; OrbitFlow commits to complete the questionnaire and answer 'no' rather than 'partially'.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: It depends on which entity the data belongs to, and that is a question for our legal team, not for you.
findings.context: Prospect's EU/German data residency requirement may not be met by OrbitFlow's EU-only offering; it depends on legal entity classification. — OrbitFlow states it has EU residency but no German region; prospect says EU may be sufficient pending legal review.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: I do not want that review sitting on the critical path of a project whose value comes from something else entirely.
findings.context: Prospect does not want generative AI in phase one because it would add data protection, works council and legal review to the critical path. — OrbitFlow says AI steps are optional and can be disabled on Enterprise; Anika wants contractual assurance that customer content is not used for training.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: I do not want to discover in year two that every occasional approver requires a full seat.
findings.context: Prospect is concerned about per-seat pricing ambiguity; wants explicit treatment of occasional approvers to avoid unexpected cost in year two. — OrbitFlow declines to give a number until the user model is known and commits to a separated, explicit proposal.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: What I care about is transparency around professional services, premium connectors, and anything we would only discover after an architecture review. That is where the surprises live.
findings.context: Prospect worries about hidden professional services and premium connector costs surfacing after architecture review. — OrbitFlow commits to price services separately and to mark unknowns as to-be-determined.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: Because a sandbox would show me the product works, and I already believe the product works. It would not tell me whether we can deploy it, and that is the open question.
findings.context: Prospect is not ready to run a sandbox; wants architecture viability proven first because a sandbox would show the product works but not whether it can be deployed. — Martin's reasoning for the next step; the decision is gated on architecture, with timing of formal review in September and production early next year.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: Regional IT cannot say no formally but can make implementation impossible, which amounts to the same thing.
findings.context: Prospect's decision involves six stakeholders, and architecture board and information security can unilaterally block; regional IT can make implementation impossible. — Martin describes the approval order; procurement is last and slow.

findings.speaker: Anika Bose
findings.quote: Regional IT will have opinions. That is not a formal gate but it is a real one. And procurement has a standard process that takes as long as it takes.
findings.context: Prospect has a procurement process that will take as long as it takes, and regional IT opinions form an informal gate. — Anika raises these as additional non-technical gates.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: There is a constraint on one of the SQL Server systems. I will find the number.
findings.context: Prospect's concern about SQL Server rate limits and throttling constraints may affect high-volume workflows. — Raised by Jon; Martin confirms a constraint exists on one SQL Server system and will find the number.

findings.speaker: Martin Vogel
findings.quote: In practice, two German plants are still prohibited from exposing production databases directly to SaaS vendors.
findings.context: Prospect's two German plants are prohibited from exposing production databases to SaaS vendors, which constrains the architecture; the policy has not been reviewed in eighteen months. — Martin corrects his earlier 'cloud-first' claim; OrbitFlow proposes deferring those plants to phase two.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: If you can't satisfy those, connector breadth will not save the project.
findings.context: Prospect's gating concerns are model risk and auditability; if these are not satisfied, connector breadth will not save the project. — Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer) framed the blockers as gates; connector breadth was described as a tie, not a differentiator.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: getting something into scope is a nine-month process here.
findings.context: Putting an AI model into a decision path would bring it under the prospect's model risk management framework, which takes about nine months. — Hannah explained the internal model-risk policy. Nina Patel responded that AI steps are explicit, optional, and can be disabled by admins, but did not fully resolve the scope concern.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: Today it's a design convention plus review, not a hard platform constraint.
findings.context: OrbitFlow's AI outputs cannot currently be enforced as leaf nodes that never feed decisions. This is a known gap, and the prospect wants it documented as a known limitation. — Vendor admitted there is no hard platform constraint; only a design convention plus review. Hannah called it a real gap and asked for it in writing.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: and that is not exportable.
findings.context: The prospect needs audit export to be programmatic and not just a UI download, and it must feed into their SIEM. — Hannah questioned what exportable means; vendor pointed to API and webhook export. Hannah accepted this only subject to seeing the payload schema.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: It's searchable. It's not auditable.
findings.context: Current exception handling is searchable but not auditable, and an auditor found the process not evidenced. This is the reason the project started. — Noah Williams described the existing Slack-and-scripts process; Hannah said this audit finding started the project.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: Retry semantics were opaque. We couldn't always tell whether something had run twice.
findings.context: Debugging large visual workflows is hard and retry semantics in the Tray PoC were opaque, making it unclear whether a step ran twice. — Prospect's reasons for finding the incumbent Tray PoC unsatisfactory; vendor agreed idempotency is a hard problem not fully solved by the platform.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: We've had integrations fail because someone renamed a field and nothing surfaced.
findings.context: Schema changes in source systems have caused past integration failures that went unnoticed, which is a concern for the new integration. — Raised as a prior failure pattern; vendor said mapping errors surface on the run and recommended validation; Hannah wants bad-data testing.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: Not currently.
findings.context: The internal event bus is not reachable from outside the network, which is a technical blocker for the required integration. — Required integration; vendor said it is a real architecture question and needs a design session.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: If the bill becomes unpredictable as volumes grow, finance will dislike it even if the base price is fine.
findings.context: Usage overages could make the second-year invoice unpredictable, and finance would dislike it even if the base price is fine. — Prior vendor experience; vendor declined to promise a cap before modelling volumes and proposed contractual overage terms.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: That's cheaper and it's what someone will propose.
findings.context: The main alternative is keeping existing scripts and documenting them better, which is cheaper and likely to be proposed internally, and could delay the project by about two months. — Hannah said it would not satisfy the auditor but could still win internal support; vendor responded by addressing it in the pilot criteria.

findings.speaker: Noah Williams
findings.quote: It's tight but it's real.
findings.context: Timeline is tight: the technical bake-off is in July and first controlled production workflows are targeted for October. — Driven by a remediation programme with a fixed date; Noah said it is tight but real.

findings.speaker: Hannah Cole
findings.quote: I said in the internal session that all approvals have to remain in Jira.
findings.context: Hannah's internal position was to keep all approvals in Jira, which she later softened to allow low-risk approvals in OrbitFlow if audit export is strong enough. — Position change; vendor confirmed scope, with high-risk approvals remaining in Jira and risk tiering to be defined by the prospect.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: Let's talk about money, because that's going to decide this.
findings.context: Prospect's main hesitation is price: the Growth package at £1,800/month is above what she had in mind. — Pricing objection raised after vendor quoted Growth package; prospect framed it as the deciding factor.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: So I'd be paying for twenty seats I don't need.
findings.context: Prospect is hesitant to pay for thirty seats when she needs about ten; she sees paying for unused seats as a cost problem. — Per-seat/package mismatch; vendor said the thirty-user package price is fixed.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: Or bill monthly while we prove the process before committing for a year?
findings.context: Annual commitment is a barrier; prospect wants monthly billing to prove the process first. Vendor's monthly availability was unconfirmed. — Prospect asked for monthly billing as a lower-risk trial; vendor said 'usually fine' and needed manager approval.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: I can sign software contracts up to twenty thousand. Above that the founder approves it.
findings.context: Spend above £20k needs founder approval, which is a hard internal limit; prospect needs a stronger value justification than 'more robust' versus Zapier at about £2k. — Internal approval barrier; prospect said the conversation upstairs will focus on ROI versus Zapier.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: We're an agency, Alastair. Nobody's auditing our onboarding process.
findings.context: Prospect questions the value of governance and audit features for an agency, undercutting the vendor's main differentiator. — Vendor leaned on governance/audit trail; prospect said nobody audits agency onboarding.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: we may well decide that Zapier plus better process discipline is good enough for a company that doesn't have an IT team.
findings.context: Prospect may choose Zapier plus better process discipline instead, given price and complexity risks and no IT team. — Competing-tool alternative raised as a real possibility; prospect said she would be doing her job badly not to consider it.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: I see it as useful but too fragile for multi-step onboarding
findings.context: Prospect is wary of the product's fit for multi-step onboarding and Zapier's fragility, though she says Zapier does about 80% of needs. — Competing-tool comparison; prospect acknowledges Zapier's value but sees it failing on branches and human steps.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: If it tells me four accounts are overdue and actually it's six, that's worse than nothing.
findings.context: Prospect doubts the AI weekly summary can be trusted for accuracy; inaccurate overdue counts would be worse than nothing. — Concern about AI accuracy; vendor deflected to 'very good' models and checking underlying data.

findings.speaker: Ben Foster
findings.quote: So if the pitch is "we'll standardise your onboarding", that's going to meet resistance from me.
findings.context: Prospect's client-services pods customise onboarding, and she expects resistance to any standardisation pitch. — Ben pushed back on the one-process framing; vendor said it's fully flexible and configurable.

findings.speaker: Ben Foster
findings.quote: And if nobody changes the record but the date just passes?
findings.context: Prospect doubts vendor's claim of no-code simplicity and timing risk for alerts that depend on date changes; vendor needed SE check. — Technical implementation concern for a team with no IT; vendor said no-code but date-slip logic might need two workflows.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: We don't have a dedicated IT team. At all.
findings.context: Prospect has no dedicated IT team and needs the tool administered by an operations manager, raising complexity concern. — Resourcing concern; vendor claimed completely no-code.

findings.speaker: Ben Foster
findings.quote: Not whether they signed.
findings.context: Prospect wants proof of customer outcomes; vendor's reference story was vague and unverified about whether the onboarding problem was solved. — Hesitation about vendor credibility; vendor said he moved off the account and 'I think' they renewed.

findings.speaker: Ben Foster
findings.quote: Because two other vendors we've spoken to had it as an enterprise-only feature and I'd be surprised if you were different.
findings.context: Prospect doubts SSO is included on all plans; two other vendors gated it to enterprise, and vendor was unconfirmed. — Security/pricing tier concern; vendor said 'fairly sure' and would confirm.

findings.speaker: Ben Foster
findings.quote: Can we see that in writing?
findings.context: Prospect requires written assurance that client documents are not used to train models, due to client sensitivity. — Security/data concern; vendor said it is in terms and would send DPA.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: I'm not ready to run a sandbox myself, I don't have the time and neither does Ben.
findings.context: Prospect is not ready to commit and wants a use-case-specific recorded demo before deciding; she lacks time to run a sandbox. — Timing/evaluation hesitation; vendor had only an unrelated demo environment earlier.

findings.speaker: Imogen Price
findings.quote: otherwise we'll build the new process around the old tooling and then we're stuck for another year.
findings.context: Prospect's timeline is driven by a September client-services launch, and she wants a running system before then; this creates urgency but also a risk of being stuck on old tooling. — Timing pressure; buyer wants to avoid building new process on old tooling.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: Yeah, that's just configuration.
findings.context: Vendor's claim of 'up and running in a couple of weeks' and 'no problem' for September and pod customisation was not verified; prospect is skeptical. — Vendor implementation claims versus prospect's needs; the customisation claim was accepted only as 'just configuration'.

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: The first-class Dynamics gap is the biggest issue for us. Power Automate is already embedded here. It's licensed, it's approved, the platform team likes it. For us to work around all of that, OrbitFlow has to be materially better, not marginally better.
findings.context: Biggest concern: OrbitFlow lacks a first-class Dynamics connector, and Power Automate is already embedded, so OrbitFlow must be materially better to justify a switch — Stated after Jon Bell candidly said OrbitFlow does not have the deepest first-class Dynamics connector; Carlos framed the gap as the core obstacle given the incumbent

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: They should not need full seats. If your model says they do, this is over before it starts.
findings.context: Per-seat licensing model could kill the deal: supervisors and approvers should not need full seats — Raised as a licensing concern; approver population (hundreds) versus builders (about six) was not yet priced; Maya declined to give a number without those counts

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: The Microsoft platform team will not want this. Not because it's bad. Because it isn't Microsoft.
findings.context: Internal approval risk: the Microsoft platform team will strongly oppose OrbitFlow because it is not Microsoft, and they have killed things before — Carlos says formal role is influence, practically depends on how strongly they object; Lucy adds they have a track record of killing tools

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: If the decision is purely cost per seat, Microsoft wins and everyone knows it.
findings.context: Cost objection: Power Automate's bundled favourable licensing makes OrbitFlow hard to justify on cost per seat; the case must rest on operational cost instead — Maya conceded Microsoft wins on pure licence cost; Carlos accepted this is the argument he would need to make internally; Maya proposed measuring the support time as a number

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: Realistically, no. I want to be straight with you about that rather than let you forecast something that isn't there.
findings.context: Timing: no decision this year; any purchase would have to fit the October budgeting cycle for next fiscal year — Carlos described the process as early exploration, explicitly not procurement, and was candid that a decision is unlikely this year

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: this is the thing that kills most vendors.
findings.context: Offline and intermittent connectivity is a hard constraint that many vendors fail on; he expects demos that assume real-time connectivity to fail — Raised by the customer as a make-or-break requirement from field sites with poor signal; Jon responded with sync-event and timeout patterns and offered a live demo

findings.speaker: Lucy Hart
findings.quote: It's more that our procurement people prefer it.
findings.context: Preference (not requirement) for UK data residency, which is unconfirmed for OrbitFlow; procurement prefers it — Jon said EU residency is available on Enterprise but UK must be confirmed; Lucy clarified it is not a regulatory mandate

findings.speaker: Carlos Mendes
findings.quote: The price might be defensible for central operations. What I need to understand is the licensing model.
findings.context: Price may be defensible for central operations, but the licensing model is the real question — Conditional acceptance of pricing (Growth at 1800/month up to 30 users; Enterprise custom); hesitation is driven by seat model rather than headline price

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: My concern — and I'd say it's the biggest risk to this whole thing — is that our security constraints plus the lack of native legal-system connectors make the integration effort disproportionate.
findings.context: Samir Khan says security constraints plus the lack of native legal-system connectors make the integration effort disproportionate to the value, calling it the biggest risk to the whole project. — Customer's main reservation, raised at the steering-meeting level. Leo responded that he would test it with an operation-by-operation difficulty assessment and a services estimate rather than argue it.

findings.speaker: Nina Patel
findings.quote: We do not have a native concept of a matter-level ethical wall that reads your barrier definitions from iManage and enforces them dynamically. That does not exist.
findings.context: Matter-level information barriers (ethical walls) are a major concern. OrbitFlow staff admitted there is no native matter-level ethical wall that reads barrier definitions from iManage and enforces them dynamically. — Customer called it 'the big one'. Nina said plainly this does not exist out of the box and that the workaround is customer-maintained design. Samir said barriers change weekly, so the maintenance burden is a real cost. Phase one was scoped to barrier-free matters as a result.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: It's not fatal. It's significant. It means every barrier change has a workflow implication, and today it doesn't.
findings.context: Samir Khan says the barrier maintenance problem is significant, not fatal, because every barrier change now has a workflow implication. — Customer's assessment after Nina's admission about barriers. Led to scoping phase one to barrier-free matters.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: For some of our clients that distinction matters a great deal.
findings.context: UK data residency is a potential deal gate. OrbitFlow only offers EU residency on Enterprise, and UK residency is unconfirmed. — Customer said some clients, especially public sector, need UK specifically. Nina would not say yes on the call and promised a written answer. Samir insisted a no must be stated as a no, not a roadmap item.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: we have a retention policy that says certain operational records are deleted at ninety days, and if your floor is above that, we have a problem.
findings.context: A customer retention policy deletes certain operational records at ninety days, so OrbitFlow's minimum retention floor could be a blocker if it is above that. — Customer raised this as a specific risk. Nina committed to checking the floor explicitly and providing numbers in the pack.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: If the workflow is handling matter data, that data ends up in your run history. Correct?
findings.context: Matter data would appear in the workflow run history, which is a security concern. Nina conceded that whatever the workflow passes between steps is visible in the run record, and that field-level masking is a design task rather than a setting. — Customer's security question. Nina was candid that there is no checkbox and the answer depends on design choices such as passing references rather than payloads.

findings.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
findings.quote: If a workflow makes a conflicts decision, we're finished.
findings.context: Conflicts decisions are a hard line. Any workflow that makes a conflicts decision would end the project. — Stated early as the firm's non-negotiable. This led Leo to propose leaving conflict approval in the existing system of record, with credential-level enforcement.

findings.speaker: Samir Khan
findings.quote: I'm much more sceptical about generative AI than Eleanor is.
findings.context: Generative AI is a reservation. Samir wants AI features disabled entirely for phase one, and Eleanor says the firm's second use case is AI-based. — Samir is more sceptical of generative AI than Eleanor. Nina confirmed AI can be disabled on Enterprise. Eleanor treats it as phase-one only and wants it kept on the table.

findings.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
findings.quote: I would not make a business case that assumes use around privileged client content, because that case would be rejected and it would poison the whole thing.
findings.context: The business case must not depend on privileged client content, because that would be rejected and would damage the whole proposal. Eleanor is wary of Enterprise pricing tied to that use. — Eleanor said the enterprise price range does not worry her. The worry is scope. Leo agreed to mark privileged-content use as out of scope, not a future upsell.

findings.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
findings.quote: If it turns out every partner needs a seat, this is a very short conversation.
findings.context: Licensing per user is a concern. If partners each need a seat, the deal becomes unviable. — Samir asked what counts as a user. Leo declined to give a number until the licence split between builders and approval-only users was clear.

findings.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
findings.quote: the counter-argument is that they then own it forever and they're already at capacity.
findings.context: Internal development is a competing alternative. Eleanor says the internal team is already at capacity and the build option would mean owning the solution indefinitely. — Samir said some people favour building in-house. Eleanor said the argument for it is that the firm understands its own systems better than a vendor.

findings.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
findings.quote: nothing significant happens here in December, and January is taken up with the annual planning cycle.
findings.context: Practice-group adoption and timing are slow. Practice groups are slow to agree to process change, and December and January are unavailable, pushing the PoC to Q4. — Eleanor said practice-group leaders must agree to any process change. Scoping to two practice groups was seen as easier. Timing is constrained by the planning cycle.

findings.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
findings.quote: So I wouldn't treat "no new interface" as an absolute requirement.
findings.context: A correction on partner interfaces: Eleanor softened her earlier position that partners do not want another interface. A simple approval dashboard might reduce email, so 'no new interface' is not an absolute requirement. — Self-correction. Samir noted it as a change. Nina then proposed a design with both email notifications and a dashboard.

findings.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
findings.quote: It does not have an API.
findings.context: The Access database used internally has no API, so it cannot be integrated and is out of scope for phase one. — Eleanor said it is one of three internal tools that matter. Nina ruled it out of phase one.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: My concern is data quality. If Salesforce fields are stale, an elegant workflow will still make bad decisions.
findings.context: Darren Wu doubts data quality: stale Salesforce fields would make the workflow make bad decisions at scale. — Data-quality objection to the proposed Zendesk+Salesforce+Snowflake workflow; Maya Chen treated it as a fair challenge and the design was adjusted to weight machine-generated signals.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: fewer than half our CSMs update the underlying fields consistently
findings.context: Account-health scores are not reliable ground truth because CSMs inconsistently update the underlying fields. — Darren challenged Olivia's reliance on health scores; Olivia partly disagreed ('directionally useful'). Darren's figure is an impression, later flagged as unmeasured (T219).

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: We could do that with SQL. We don't need a workflow platform to do that.
findings.context: Prospect would first validate whether the signal exists in historical data before buying, and sees a SQL analysis as possibly sufficient without a workflow platform. — Hesitation about buying a workflow platform before proof. Jon Bell agreed and recommended doing the backward analysis first.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: Absence of escalation isn't the same as fine.
findings.context: Absence of escalation cannot be used to infer an account was fine, so false-positive rates are hard to measure. — Measurement concern about the backward analysis; Jon Bell said this applies to any approach, including Gainsight, and is not OrbitFlow-specific.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: It's the alternative I'd propose if the cost comparison favoured it.
findings.context: Expanding the existing Gainsight deployment is the competing alternative the prospect would consider if cost favours it. — Competitive objection. Maya Chen said the comparison should be done honestly rather than ignoring the competition.

findings.speaker: Olivia Grant
findings.quote: because the forty-percent thing wasn't a licensing failure, it was an implementation failure.
findings.context: Prior Gainsight shortfall was an implementation failure, not a licensing failure, so the cost comparison must include implementation effort. — Olivia wants implementation effort on both sides of the comparison; Maya agreed to build it that way.

findings.speaker: Olivia Grant
findings.quote: I think the price is reasonable if it lets us consolidate several manual programmes.
findings.context: Price is acceptable only if the platform consolidates several manual programmes; Gainsight spend is also questioned. — Conditional price acceptance. Olivia said the Gainsight spend is questionable, and Darren said that is a separate fight; Maya did not want to be in the middle.

findings.speaker: Olivia Grant
findings.quote: I don't want to find out in month four that all sixty-two need full seats.
findings.context: Concern that per-seat licensing could be much higher than expected if all CSM task recipients need full seats. — About 60-62 CSMs receive tasks versus 3-4 builders. Maya said the split would be itemised in the proposal and no figure was quoted on the call.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: We'd need to be able to say the intervention caused the renewal, and we can't.
findings.context: The renewal-retention ROI case depends on a counterfactual that cannot be proven, so finance is sceptical. — Darren raised this against Olivia's ROI argument; Maya suggested time-to-first-intervention as a measurable leading indicator instead.

findings.speaker: Olivia Grant
findings.quote: Finance can say not yet, which is the same thing in practice.
findings.context: Finance and security have effective veto power; Darren would block if the data does not support the project. — Internal approval hurdles. Olivia said Finance saying not yet is equivalent to no in practice.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: I'd say no if the data doesn't support it.
findings.context: Darren would say no if the data does not support the project. — Conditional objection tied to the backward-looking data analysis.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: Salesforce, no. Salesforce fields get overwritten, there's no history on most of them.
findings.context: Historical Salesforce data is not available for point-in-time backtesting because fields are overwritten. — Data limitation for the 20-escalation pilot; Jon Bell noted it agrees with the design decision to exclude human-maintained fields.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: our position is that they should never leave our warehouse.
findings.context: Student-level data must never leave the warehouse (FERPA); the vendor must not access student records. — Compliance boundary. Jon Bell said defining it in the Snowflake view makes it impossible rather than forbidden. Darren said a full vendor security review is still needed.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: I'm not having business-critical logic that only exists in a web UI.
findings.context: Workflow logic must be reviewable and version-controlled, not only in a web UI. — Jon Bell said there is version history and API export but it is not a git integration and a true diff is unconfirmed.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: I want to know that if I get hit by a bus, someone else can pick this up.
findings.context: Key-person dependency risk: the project could be lost if its owner leaves, as happened with Gainsight. — Jon Bell said this is mostly an operating-model issue, not a product answer.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: If there isn't a theme this week, will it invent one?
findings.context: Concern that the AI weekly summary could invent themes when none exist. — Jon Bell said the workflow should refuse thin cases via minimum-evidence rules rather than relying on model confidence.

findings.speaker: Olivia Grant
findings.quote: We want a pilot before the November renewal planning cycle, with a decision by late September.
findings.context: Timing constraint: pilot must happen before the November renewal planning cycle, with a decision by late September, and August is the window. — Calendar-driven deadline; term starts early September with CSMs unavailable for two weeks. Missing November means waiting until March.

findings.speaker: Ava Sinclair
findings.quote: What I do not want is to pay you per event.
findings.context: Prospect's main hesitation is that usage-based pricing on high-volume event processing could make the product uneconomic versus keeping event handling in AWS; she does not want to pay per event. — Cost/pricing objection raised early, then tied to volume; OrbitFlow staff responded by recommending filtering upstream and said the design avoids per-event cost.

findings.speaker: Ava Sinclair
findings.quote: If I emit a business event and it triggers a workflow that fans out to five subflows, is that one run or six?
findings.context: Prospect is concerned that a subflow fan-out might be billed as multiple runs, which would make the recommended composition pattern expensive. — Pricing concern; OrbitFlow rep could not confirm billing semantics from memory and promised a written answer.

findings.speaker: Ava Sinclair
findings.quote: I think most of what you do could be built internally. We have the skills. The question is whether we should.
findings.context: Prospect's core reservation is that building internally with Step Functions or Retool Workflows is a credible alternative, and that maintenance ownership is the real cost. — Build-vs-buy objection; the sponsor (Marcus) argued maintenance is the real cost and the person who would own it is overloaded.

findings.speaker: Ava Sinclair
findings.quote: I've also seen teams buy a platform to avoid maintenance and then spend a year maintaining the integration to the platform.
findings.context: Prospect worries that teams buy a platform to avoid maintenance and then spend a year maintaining the integration to it. — Maintenance-cost concern; OrbitFlow agreed it happens and proposed testing time consumed over four weeks.

findings.speaker: Marcus Chen
findings.quote: If we end up with something only Ava understands, we've spent money to move the problem.
findings.context: Prospect's sponsor is worried the workflows will be understandable only by the engineer, which would move the problem rather than solve it. — Comprehensibility and adoption concern; OrbitFlow admitted complex canvases are unreadable by default and that there is no linter enforcing composition.

findings.speaker: Ava Sinclair
findings.quote: We have EU customers and a data residency commitment in some contracts. So EU residency is probably the requirement.
findings.context: Prospect has EU data residency commitments in enterprise contracts, which is a gating requirement; the sponsor was unsure how many contracts exist. — Security/compliance requirement; OrbitFlow said EU residency is Enterprise-only and advised checking before evaluation.

findings.speaker: Ava Sinclair
findings.quote: Salesforce API limits are the constraint. We've hit them before.
findings.context: Prospect names the Salesforce API limits as a hard constraint that could block the design; they have hit them before. — Integration/rate-limit concern; OrbitFlow proposed batching or caching if the allocation is insufficient.

findings.speaker: Ava Sinclair
findings.quote: If the exported definitions turn out to be unreadable. If subflows are billed individually and the economics invert. And if the Postgres connector does something stupid.
findings.context: Prospect lists stated blockers: unreadable exported definitions, subflows billed individually, and a Postgres connector that misbehaves. — Explicit list of deal-breakers; the sponsor asked what would block it.

draft.answer: Across all 10 Prospect calls, the most recurring hesitations were pricing and licensing, especially per-seat surprises [C1][C2]. Security, compliance and data-residency gates also recurred, including written no-training commitments and AI exclusion from phase one [C3][C4]. Prospects also named status quo or existing tools as the real alternative and raised internal approval and timing hurdles [C5][C6]. Integration and architecture fit and maintenance or adoption risk came up as well [C7][C8].

claims.text: Price level and ROI justification were raised in many calls. Acme Logistics said price was above expectation and wanted a clearer ROI story. Cedar & Finch expected $800-1,000 versus $1,800/month. Fable Media's Imogen Price called price the deciding factor, said she would pay for about 20 unneeded seats, and wanted monthly billing. Greenline said Power Automate wins on cost per seat. Juniper does not want to pay per event.

Per-seat licensing surprises for occasional approvers were raised independently at Acme Logistics, BrightPath Health, DeltaWorks, Greenline, Harbor Legal and Inkwell, and at Greenline and Harbor they were deal-ending ('over before it starts', 'very short conversation'). Hidden usage, overage and services costs worried Cedar & Finch, DeltaWorks, Ember and Juniper (subflow billing).

Security and compliance gates: BrightPath said the BAA is a hard gate and that price is irrelevant until it is resolved. DeltaWorks has a 240-question questionnaire and works council delay risk. Harbor Legal raised ethical walls and UK residency. EU or UK data residency came up at BrightPath, Cedar & Finch, DeltaWorks, Harbor, Greenline and Juniper. Written or contractual no-training assurance was demanded at Acme, BrightPath and Fable.

Several prospects wanted generative AI excluded or deferred from phase one (BrightPath, DeltaWorks, Harbor Legal, Acme). Ember said an AI model in a decision path triggers a nine-month model-risk process. Others doubted AI accuracy (Fable, Inkwell) or distrusted agents (Acme).

Status quo or existing tools were named as the real alternative: Workato at Acme, Power Automate at BrightPath and Greenline, Zapier at Cedar & Finch and Fable, keeping scripts at Ember, Gainsight at Inkwell, and in-house builds at Harbor Legal and Juniper (Step Functions or Retool).

Internal approval and timing hurdles: Cedar & Finch can only approve under $15k/year and the $21.6k cost goes to the COO and finance director. Fable needs founder approval above £20k. Greenline's Microsoft platform team will likely oppose, and no decision is expected this year. BrightPath has no production launch before Q4. DeltaWorks has six stakeholders who can block. Inkwell's finance has effective veto.

Integration and architecture fit worried several prospects: DeltaWorks (on-premise and SAP reachability, German plants), Ember (event bus not reachable, schema changes), Greenline (no first-class Dynamics connector, offline connectivity), Cedar & Finch (Shopify trigger must be native) and Juniper (Salesforce API limits). Harbor Legal said integration effort could be disproportionate.

Maintenance, ownership and adoption risk: Acme feared a tool the team must babysit, and its operators must believe they can own it. BrightPath feared users would route around workflows. Inkwell raised key-person dependency, and Juniper's sponsor feared only the engineer would understand the workflows.

not_covered: No frequency count per reason was computed; ranking reflects how many calls raised each theme, based on the findings listed.
assumptions: Only Prospect call type (new business) is included, per the stated assumption.
Theme ordering is read from the findings, not from code-computed counts.

evidence.quote: It's more than I expected. And I know why — I'd mentally benchmarked this against Zapier, which is not a fair comparison
evidence.context: Pricing was higher than the prospect expected, anchored on Zapier as a benchmark. — Customer framed it as more than expected; acknowledged the Zapier comparison is unfair but still the number in her head. Vendor responded by deferring a number until user model is known.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah

evidence.speaker: Anika Bose

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes

evidence.speaker: Anika Bose
evidence.quote: Six is realistic if the use case is contested.

evidence.speaker: Elliot Greene
evidence.quote: We're a US operation with a UK subsidiary. What's the default region?

evidence.speaker: Lucy Hart
evidence.quote: It's more that our procurement people prefer it.
evidence.context: Preference (not requirement) for UK data residency, which is unconfirmed for OrbitFlow; procurement prefers it — Jon said EU residency is available on Enterprise but UK must be confirmed; Lucy clarified it is not a regulatory mandate

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: We have EU customers and a data residency commitment in some contracts. So EU residency is probably the requirement.
evidence.context: Prospect has EU data residency commitments in enterprise contracts, which is a gating requirement; the sponsor was unsure how many contracts exist. — Security/compliance requirement; OrbitFlow said EU residency is Enterprise-only and advised checking before evaluation.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: That last one needs to be in writing. Not in a demo.
evidence.context: Prospect requires that no-training on customer workflow content be documented in writing, not just stated in a demo. — Condition for trust; vendor agreed it belongs in the contract.

evidence.speaker: Elliot Greene
evidence.quote: That last sentence. Is it in the contract or is it on a marketing page?
evidence.context: Prospect wants a no-training commitment to be contractual, not just marketing-page language. — Vendor said it 'needs to be in the contract for you to rely on it'; Elliot said he will insist on that.

evidence.speaker: Ben Foster
evidence.quote: Can we see that in writing?
evidence.context: Prospect requires written assurance that client documents are not used to train models, due to client sensitivity. — Security/data concern; vendor said it is in terms and would send DPA.

claims.text: Several prospects wanted generative AI excluded or deferred from phase one (BrightPath, DeltaWorks, Harbor Legal, Acme). Ember said an AI model in a decision path triggers a nine-month model-risk process. Others doubted AI accuracy (Fable, Inkwell) or distrusted agents (Acme).

evidence.speaker: Elliot Greene
evidence.quote: The second one. That separation would help a lot, actually. AI is interesting but it's not worth blocking the automation use case over.
evidence.context: Prospect's concern about LLM/AI data handling was significant enough to want AI excluded from phase one; they accepted deferring AI review to a separate track. — Elliot called it 'the one I actually care about'. Vendor offered disabling AI or scoping phase one to deterministic steps. Priya noted it was a bigger concession than usual.

evidence.speaker: Anika Bose
evidence.quote: I do not want that review sitting on the critical path of a project whose value comes from something else entirely.
evidence.context: Prospect does not want generative AI in phase one because it would add data protection, works council and legal review to the critical path. — OrbitFlow says AI steps are optional and can be disabled on Enterprise; Anika wants contractual assurance that customer content is not used for training.

evidence.speaker: Samir Khan
evidence.quote: I'm much more sceptical about generative AI than Eleanor is.
evidence.context: Generative AI is a reservation. Samir wants AI features disabled entirely for phase one, and Eleanor says the firm's second use case is AI-based. — Samir is more sceptical of generative AI than Eleanor. Nina confirmed AI can be disabled on Enterprise. Eleanor treats it as phase-one only and wants it kept on the table.

evidence.speaker: Tom Alvarez
evidence.quote: AI's interesting but it's not worth blocking the automation case over.
evidence.context: Security review is not a blocker; AI usage and LLM data handling may need separate review and could be scoped out. — Customer said separation would help and AI is not worth blocking automation; vendor offered to disable AI or scope pilot to deterministic steps.

evidence.speaker: Hannah Cole
evidence.quote: getting something into scope is a nine-month process here.
evidence.context: Putting an AI model into a decision path would bring it under the prospect's model risk management framework, which takes about nine months. — Hannah explained the internal model-risk policy. Nina Patel responded that AI steps are explicit, optional, and can be disabled by admins, but did not fully resolve the scope concern.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: If it tells me four accounts are overdue and actually it's six, that's worse than nothing.
evidence.context: Prospect doubts the AI weekly summary can be trusted for accuracy; inaccurate overdue counts would be worse than nothing. — Concern about AI accuracy; vendor deflected to 'very good' models and checking underlying data.

evidence.speaker: Darren Wu
evidence.quote: If there isn't a theme this week, will it invent one?
evidence.context: Concern that the AI weekly summary could invent themes when none exist. — Jon Bell said the workflow should refuse thin cases via minimum-evidence rules rather than relying on model confidence.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: I'm wary of the word agent, mostly because it usually means nobody can explain why something happened.
evidence.context: Prospect is wary of AI agents because they can obscure why something happened. — Reservation about agent-style AI; vendor framed AI as optional, inspectable steps.

claims.text: Status quo or existing tools were named as the real alternative: Workato at Acme, Power Automate at BrightPath and Greenline, Zapier at Cedar & Finch and Fable, keeping scripts at Ember, Gainsight at Inkwell, and in-house builds at Harbor Legal and Juniper (Step Functions or Retool).

evidence.speaker: Tom Alvarez
evidence.quote: And the honest comparison is Workato, or just improving what we already have. Not doing nothing.
evidence.context: Status quo (Workato or improving existing process) is the honest comparison, and 'do nothing' is not the alternative. — Customer and vendor agreed the pilot should be defined against status quo and alternatives; vendor said 'don't buy OrbitFlow' is a valid outcome.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: Power Automate. Or just improving what we already have.
evidence.context: Status quo and Microsoft Power Automate are the real competitors; Power Automate is already covered by their Microsoft agreement, which matters to procurement. — Vendor said a 'don't buy' outcome is valid if the existing approach meets criteria more cheaply. Earlier Priya said Power Automate is already covered by the Microsoft agreement.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: The first-class Dynamics gap is the biggest issue for us. Power Automate is already embedded here. It's licensed, it's approved, the platform team likes it. For us to work around all of that, OrbitFlow has to be materially better, not marginally better.
evidence.context: Biggest concern: OrbitFlow lacks a first-class Dynamics connector, and Power Automate is already embedded, so OrbitFlow must be materially better to justify a switch — Stated after Jon Bell candidly said OrbitFlow does not have the deepest first-class Dynamics connector; Carlos framed the gap as the core obstacle given the incumbent

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: budget is the biggest risk here. We could decide we're simply over-buying, and keep Zapier while improving documentation and ownership.
evidence.context: Budget is the biggest risk; prospect may conclude they are over-buying and keep Zapier with better documentation and ownership. — Sophie framed a no-buy outcome as legitimate; Leo said he'd rather learn that in July than month five.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: we may well decide that Zapier plus better process discipline is good enough for a company that doesn't have an IT team.
evidence.context: Prospect may choose Zapier plus better process discipline instead, given price and complexity risks and no IT team. — Competing-tool alternative raised as a real possibility; prospect said she would be doing her job badly not to consider it.

evidence.speaker: Noah Williams
evidence.quote: That's cheaper and it's what someone will propose.
evidence.context: The main alternative is keeping existing scripts and documenting them better, which is cheaper and likely to be proposed internally, and could delay the project by about two months. — Hannah said it would not satisfy the auditor but could still win internal support; vendor responded by addressing it in the pilot criteria.

evidence.speaker: Darren Wu
evidence.quote: It's the alternative I'd propose if the cost comparison favoured it.
evidence.context: Expanding the existing Gainsight deployment is the competing alternative the prospect would consider if cost favours it. — Competitive objection. Maya Chen said the comparison should be done honestly rather than ignoring the competition.

evidence.speaker: Eleanor Brooks
evidence.quote: the counter-argument is that they then own it forever and they're already at capacity.
evidence.context: Internal development is a competing alternative. Eleanor says the internal team is already at capacity and the build option would mean owning the solution indefinitely. — Samir said some people favour building in-house. Eleanor said the argument for it is that the firm understands its own systems better than a vendor.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: I think most of what you do could be built internally. We have the skills. The question is whether we should.
evidence.context: Prospect's core reservation is that building internally with Step Functions or Retool Workflows is a credible alternative, and that maintenance ownership is the real cost. — Build-vs-buy objection; the sponsor (Marcus) argued maintenance is the real cost and the person who would own it is overloaded.

claims.text: Internal approval and timing hurdles: Cedar & Finch can only approve under $15k/year and the $21.6k cost goes to the COO and finance director. Fable needs founder approval above £20k. Greenline's Microsoft platform team will likely oppose, and no decision is expected this year. BrightPath has no production launch before Q4. DeltaWorks has six stakeholders who can block. Inkwell's finance has effective veto.

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: Above that it goes to the COO and the finance director.
evidence.context: Budget approval threshold: prospect can only approve tools under $15k/year; the $21.6k annual cost goes to COO and finance director, a slower process. — Internal approval hesitation; the buyer's stated reason for delay.

evidence.speaker: Imogen Price
evidence.quote: I can sign software contracts up to twenty thousand. Above that the founder approves it.
evidence.context: Spend above £20k needs founder approval, which is a hard internal limit; prospect needs a stronger value justification than 'more robust' versus Zapier at about £2k. — Internal approval barrier; prospect said the conversation upstairs will focus on ROI versus Zapier.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: The Microsoft platform team will not want this. Not because it's bad. Because it isn't Microsoft.
evidence.context: Internal approval risk: the Microsoft platform team will strongly oppose OrbitFlow because it is not Microsoft, and they have killed things before — Carlos says formal role is influence, practically depends on how strongly they object; Lucy adds they have a track record of killing tools

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: Realistically, no. I want to be straight with you about that rather than let you forecast something that isn't there.
evidence.context: Timing: no decision this year; any purchase would have to fit the October budgeting cycle for next fiscal year — Carlos described the process as early exploration, explicitly not procurement, and was candid that a decision is unlikely this year

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: No production launch before Q4. That's firm.
evidence.context: Timing constraint: no production launch before Q4; only a non-sensitive proof of concept is possible sooner. A successful pilot would not automatically mean broad deployment. — Priya said pilot and broad deployment are two decisions with different approvers. Vendor said it would rather hear this now.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: Regional IT cannot say no formally but can make implementation impossible, which amounts to the same thing.
evidence.context: Prospect's decision involves six stakeholders, and architecture board and information security can unilaterally block; regional IT can make implementation impossible. — Martin describes the approval order; procurement is last and slow.

evidence.speaker: Olivia Grant
evidence.quote: Finance can say not yet, which is the same thing in practice.
evidence.context: Finance and security have effective veto power; Darren would block if the data does not support the project. — Internal approval hurdles. Olivia said Finance saying not yet is equivalent to no in practice.

claims.text: Integration and architecture fit worried several prospects: DeltaWorks (on-premise and SAP reachability, German plants), Ember (event bus not reachable, schema changes), Greenline (no first-class Dynamics connector, offline connectivity), Cedar & Finch (Shopify trigger must be native) and Juniper (Salesforce API limits). Harbor Legal said integration effort could be disproportionate.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: Because if the deployment architecture doesn't work, the product is irrelevant. We have bought software before that demonstrated beautifully and then could not reach our systems.
evidence.context: Prospect hesitates on deployment architecture: systems that cannot be exposed to the public internet cannot be reached by a platform calling over the internet. — Martin frames this as a gating concern; Jon responds that an agent or controlled gateway pattern may work but must be validated against the actual environment.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: the biggest issue is whether SAP and our on-premise systems make the implementation too heavy for the first use case. Everything else is manageable.
evidence.context: Prospect states the biggest issue is whether SAP and on-premise systems make implementation too heavy for the first use case; this is the crux of the decision. — Martin says everything else is manageable; if integration needs nine months of work, he would choose a different first use case or not proceed.

evidence.speaker: Martin Vogel
evidence.quote: In practice, two German plants are still prohibited from exposing production databases directly to SaaS vendors.
evidence.context: Prospect's two German plants are prohibited from exposing production databases to SaaS vendors, which constrains the architecture; the policy has not been reviewed in eighteen months. — Martin corrects his earlier 'cloud-first' claim; OrbitFlow proposes deferring those plants to phase two.

evidence.speaker: Noah Williams
evidence.quote: Not currently.
evidence.context: The internal event bus is not reachable from outside the network, which is a technical blocker for the required integration. — Required integration; vendor said it is a real architecture question and needs a design session.

evidence.speaker: Hannah Cole
evidence.quote: We've had integrations fail because someone renamed a field and nothing surfaced.
evidence.context: Schema changes in source systems have caused past integration failures that went unnoticed, which is a concern for the new integration. — Raised as a prior failure pattern; vendor said mapping errors surface on the run and recommended validation; Hannah wants bad-data testing.

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: The first-class Dynamics gap is the biggest issue for us. Power Automate is already embedded here. It's licensed, it's approved, the platform team likes it. For us to work around all of that, OrbitFlow has to be materially better, not marginally better.
evidence.context: Biggest concern: OrbitFlow lacks a first-class Dynamics connector, and Power Automate is already embedded, so OrbitFlow must be materially better to justify a switch — Stated after Jon Bell candidly said OrbitFlow does not have the deepest first-class Dynamics connector; Carlos framed the gap as the core obstacle given the incumbent

evidence.speaker: Carlos Mendes
evidence.quote: this is the thing that kills most vendors.
evidence.context: Offline and intermittent connectivity is a hard constraint that many vendors fail on; he expects demos that assume real-time connectivity to fail — Raised by the customer as a make-or-break requirement from field sites with poor signal; Jon responded with sync-event and timeout patterns and offered a live demo

evidence.speaker: Sophie Reed
evidence.quote: If that's a polling hack I'm not interested.
evidence.context: Shopify trigger must be native and event-driven; a polling workaround is a dealbreaker. Vendor could not confirm trigger coverage and deferred to a written answer. — Integration concern; vendor did not confirm.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: Salesforce API limits are the constraint. We've hit them before.
evidence.context: Prospect names the Salesforce API limits as a hard constraint that could block the design; they have hit them before. — Integration/rate-limit concern; OrbitFlow proposed batching or caching if the allocation is insufficient.

evidence.speaker: Samir Khan
evidence.quote: My concern — and I'd say it's the biggest risk to this whole thing — is that our security constraints plus the lack of native legal-system connectors make the integration effort disproportionate.
evidence.context: Samir Khan says security constraints plus the lack of native legal-system connectors make the integration effort disproportionate to the value, calling it the biggest risk to the whole project. — Customer's main reservation, raised at the steering-meeting level. Leo responded that he would test it with an operation-by-operation difficulty assessment and a services estimate rather than argue it.

claims.text: Maintenance, ownership and adoption risk: Acme feared a tool the team must babysit, and its operators must believe they can own it. BrightPath feared users would route around workflows. Inkwell raised key-person dependency, and Juniper's sponsor feared only the engineer would understand the workflows.

evidence.speaker: Tom Alvarez
evidence.quote: I want to make sure we don't buy a tool that looks great in a demo and then becomes another thing my team has to babysit.
evidence.context: Concern that a demo looks great but becomes another thing the team must babysit; wary of hidden scaling and fragility. — Customer's concern about tools that become maintenance burdens and depend on individuals; vendor pointed to run history and ownership features.

evidence.speaker: Rachel Morgan
evidence.quote: And the people who'll operate it have to believe they can own it — that last one is not a small thing.
evidence.context: Prospect expects the decision to slip and wants the operating team to believe they can own the workflow. — Timing concern: choose vendor by end of July, first workflows live in September; customer says it will slip. Ownership by operators is a key decision condition.

evidence.speaker: Priya Shah
evidence.quote: A technically correct workflow that everyone routes around is a failed implementation.
evidence.context: Prospect worries that adoption will fail, with users routing around a technically correct workflow, as happened with a previous internal tool. — Raised in the pilot-measurement discussion; Priya wants adoption measured alongside technical success.

evidence.speaker: Darren Wu
evidence.quote: I want to know that if I get hit by a bus, someone else can pick this up.
evidence.context: Key-person dependency risk: the project could be lost if its owner leaves, as happened with Gainsight. — Jon Bell said this is mostly an operating-model issue, not a product answer.

evidence.speaker: Ava Sinclair
evidence.quote: I've also seen teams buy a platform to avoid maintenance and then spend a year maintaining the integration to the platform.
evidence.context: Prospect worries that teams buy a platform to avoid maintenance and then spend a year maintaining the integration to it. — Maintenance-cost concern; OrbitFlow agreed it happens and proposed testing time consumed over four weeks.

evidence.speaker: Marcus Chen
evidence.quote: If we end up with something only Ava understands, we've spent money to move the problem.
evidence.context: Prospect's sponsor is worried the workflows will be understandable only by the engineer, which would move the problem rather than solve it. — Comprehensibility and adoption concern; OrbitFlow admitted complex canvases are unreadable by default and that there is no linter enforcing composition.

not_covered: No frequency count per reason was computed; ranking reflects how many calls raised each theme, based on the findings listed.
assumptions: 'Prospects' interpreted as Prospect call type (new business) only, excluding Renewal, Churn post-mortem, and Cold call calls.
'Most common' requires aggregating reasons across calls, so each call is read for its underlying stated objections rather than for a frequency count.
Only Prospect call type (new business) is included, per the stated assumption.
Theme ordering is read from the findings, not from code-computed counts.
